h: Ramlila Maidan: nineteen parties, one roar, and the question of whether a crowd can beat a machine
dek: On 1 November, the largest opposition crowd in years filled Delhi's Ramlila Maidan. The demand was a single one: the chief election commissioner's resignation. But the speeches carried three different politics: one called the 2024 election illegal, one looked to 2027, and one questioned everything from EVMs to the counting of votes.
pub: From reports in The Wire, Amar Ujala, Tehelka Hindi and The New Indian Express
body: Even the road to Ramlila Maidan looked like a rally on its own. Open jeeps moved through the middle of Delhi, from Minto Road to Ajmeri Gate, one after another. In the lead vehicle sat Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, Akhilesh Yadav, Mamata Banerjee, Tejashwi Yadav, Mehbooba Mufti, Farooq Abdullah and the general secretaries of the Left parties. Crowds lined both sides of the road, the tricolour and party flags in their hands. The rally had one declared demand: the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. But for the people who had gathered, this was never only about a post falling vacant.

On Sunday, 1 November, Ramlila Maidan saw a sight that years of electoral fatigue had made people stop expecting. The count of parties reached nineteen. Supporters came by train and bus from Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Bengal and Maharashtra. Delhi Police said more than four thousand personnel and over two hundred CCTV cameras had been deployed. The rally ran nearly four hours and eight leaders spoke from the stage. But the real story was not the words spoken from the stage. It was the scene that held through the speeches: people sitting on the ground, children on shoulders, and the echo of slogans between every sentence.

The rally was tied directly to the symbolic impeachment held a day earlier, staged by the opposition at Kharge's residence at 10 Rajaji Marg like a mock parliament. There it was said that Gyanesh Kumar had rebelled against the Constitution. On Sunday that charge was repeated on the street. In the past twenty-five days the opposition had come together on this issue for the seventh time. The rally was not the anger of one day, then, but the product of a month of sustained politics.

What Rahul Gandhi said from the stage became the sharpest political line of the day. He called the 2024 Lok Sabha election illegal and stolen, and claimed that according to the Election Commission's own figures 13.3 crore voters had been struck off the rolls, one in every seven. That number is Rahul's claim, not the commission's, and the commission has already rejected it. He then said what became the day's headline: Gyanesh Kumar will be removed as CEC, he will go to jail, and after him will come the turn of Amit Shah and Narendra Modi. He called this no ordinary theft but the theft of every citizen's voice, and in the language of the law described it as one of the rarest of rare cases.

It was a shared stage, but every party brought its own language. Kharge said it was not just the election commission but the prime minister himself who had to go, and called the governments at the Centre, in Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra governments of theft. Mamata Banerjee turned the Bengal results around in one line: we did not lose, we were made to lose. Akhilesh Yadav called Ramlila Maidan the Haldighati of democracy and said those who came from Uttar Pradesh would be given a farewell from Uttar Pradesh. Tejashwi Yadav compared the stage to the Mahabharata, spoke of Shakuni's dice, and asked straight questions: who was given the contract for the voter-roll software, and where are its documents?

It was also clear that this rally was not only the politics of opposing power but preparation for the next election. Assembly elections are due in Uttar Pradesh next year, and in Punjab and Uttarakhand too. Both Akhilesh and Tejashwi tied the voter-roll issue directly to those elections. The Left parties asked the young and Gen Z to lead the movement. The opposition, in other words, wants to make the voter roll not just a matter of fighting the commission but the central issue of the next election.

Politics was running outside the rally too that day. The Aam Aadmi Party and the DMK, which are no longer part of the INDIA bloc, were not on the stage, though both have separately condemned the SIR. The Cockroach Janta Party had backed the rally but did not come to the stage. The BJP held a 'Save Democracy, Remove Anarchy' march in Delhi the same day and attacked the opposition for holding a rally on the anniversary of the 1984 anti-Sikh riots. Home Minister Amit Shah said in Chandigarh that instructions for the rally had come from abroad, and alleged that Rahul Gandhi had rubbed salt into the wounds of riot victims. BJP president J. P. Nadda repeated the charge.

The rally showed both the politics of the crowd and the intensity of the speeches, but the real test is still ahead. The opposition has to prove that the charges of deletions from the voter roll are not just a count of speeches but a story with evidence on the ground, and that this fight is connected to the people whose names were struck off first. The government, on the other hand, has to explain why the figures keep changing if everything is transparent, and why dissenting letters are being written from inside the commission itself. Today's question is the same: can a crowd shake an institution like the Election Commission? The answer lies not only in the next election results but in how much trust an ordinary voter feels on seeing his own name on the roll.
nazar: The rally's biggest achievement was that it made the grievances of different states stand on one stage: Bengal's sixteen lakh appeals, Uttar Pradesh's deleted names, Bihar's complaints about the counting. A shared conversation took shape, and that is its strength. The delicate part is the outcome: policy pressure only builds when anger on the street turns into paper. Otherwise a rally's effect shrinks by the next rally.

If Rahul's figure of 13.3 crore is proved by the commission's own documents, it will become the biggest question ever asked of India's electoral system. And if it is not proved, the government will get the easiest weapon with which to dismiss the opposition. That is why the most important work of this rally is not the speech but the document.
sawal: Can the politics of the crowd shake an institution like the Election Commission, or do only the courts and documents count?
ref: Special Intensive Revision (SIR)
The special review of the voter roll in which names are checked house to house. The charge is that a large number of valid voters were struck off, especially workers, Dalits, Muslims and migrants.
Public impeachment

On 31 October the opposition called a symbolic parliament at 10 Rajaji Marg, where charges of rebelling against the Constitution were made against the chief election commissioner. It was not a legal proceeding but a political spectacle.
INDIA bloc
The opposition front formed before the 2024 Lok Sabha election. The Aam Aadmi Party and the DMK have since left it, but they oppose the SIR.

h: Rahul Gandhi: Gyanesh Kumar will go to jail, and after him it is your turn
dek: From the stage Rahul announced a three-step sequence: first the chief election commissioner, then the home minister, and then the prime minister. He called the 2024 election stolen and described vote theft as the theft of every citizen's voice.
body: Rahul Gandhi began his speech where he had left off a day earlier in the mock parliament. He said from the stage that what he says comes true. What I said about Covid came true. Now I am saying this: Gyanesh Kumar will be removed from the post of chief election commissioner and will go to jail. That sentence became the sharpest news of the day and set the tone for the whole rally.

Rahul's argument had three parts. The first was the numbers. He said the Election Commission had removed 13.3 crore voters from the roll, about fifteen per cent of the country's electorate, one in every seven. According to him the gap between the ruling alliance and the opposition in 2024 was three per cent, and so that election was illegal and stolen. The number is his claim; the commission has already rejected it.

The second part was legal. He said vote theft is not ordinary theft, not a few things taken from a shop. It is the theft of the voice of every citizen of India. In the language of the law, he said, this is called one of the rarest of rare cases. He said that without Gyanesh Kumar neither Narendra Modi would have become prime minister nor Amit Shah home minister. And then he warned the two directly: after Gyanesh Kumar it is your turn, legal action will follow, you cannot run.

The third part was about institutions. Rahul said the RSS had captured every institution: education, health, the CBI, the ED, the judiciary, the bureaucracy and the police. He said these institutions do not belong to Modi, Shah or the RSS but to the country's young people, and they have to be taken back. He tied this to economic inequality: farmers are not getting their rights, the young are not getting jobs, workers are not getting their due, and the country's wealth is flowing into the hands of two or three people. Big industrialists have thousands of crores in loans written off, while the poor have to suffer humiliation to get a loan.

Rahul also answered the prime minister's remark that Modi is not going anywhere. He said Amit Shah says Modi is not going anywhere; I say the opposite, Modi cannot go anywhere. Even if he wants to leave, we will not let him. That sentence became the sharpest political clash of the day.

What is worth noting is that Rahul linked the charges about the voter roll directly to the question of power. The fight is no longer confined to the Election Commission; it has reached the prime minister and the home minister. That was the rally's biggest political leap, and also its biggest risk.
nazar: This time Rahul did not leave his speech at accusations; he put them in a sequence: first the election commissioner, then the home minister, then the prime minister. The sequence itself is his political message, that this is not a fight for one resignation but about the character of power. But the clearer the sequence, the more the evidence matters.

If the figure of 13.3 crore is not proved by the commission's documents, the government will dismiss it most easily and the real issue will slip behind. Rahul's next test, then, is not the intensity of his speech but the confirmation of his number.
sawal: Can legal action against an election commissioner be announced from a stage, or is this only political language?
ref: Rarest of rare

In the language of the courts this phrase is used for the few cases where the severity of punishment is highest. By citing it Rahul tried to place vote theft in the category of the most serious crimes.

h: Kharge: governments of theft, and democracy will survive only if Modi goes
dek: The Congress president spoke the most aggressive language of the rally. He called the governments at the Centre, in Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra governments of theft, and said Gyanesh Kumar would be dug out even from the netherworld.
body: Mallikarjun Kharge was the most senior leader on the stage that day, and he chose the most direct language, in keeping with his age and experience. He said it was not only the election commission but the prime minister himself who had to be removed, because democracy will not survive until Modi goes. He repeated the sentence again and again, as if he wanted to make it the slogan of the whole rally.

Kharge's main charge was that the BJP chooses its voters; the people do not choose it. He said the government at the Centre, the government in Bihar, the government in Uttar Pradesh and the government in Maharashtra were all governments of theft. According to him the ruling side was playing with the votes of women, the young and Dalits, and using agencies like the ED to frighten the opposition.

He said we are not the ones who get frightened, whether you set the ED on us or the CBI. We all know how to fight. Then he said the sentence that was remembered all day: even if Gyanesh Kumar goes down to the netherworld, we will dig him out from there too. He also said the opposition would force his resignation and pursue a case against him.

Kharge said at the rally that the prime minister was trying to divide the country and to snatch people's votes. He said the movement would continue until the BJP was removed from power, and that Modi would go only when people fought strongly.

Kharge's language was seen as the biggest political event of the day, because on one side he is the Congress president and on the other he spoke for the whole opposition. He tied the Election Commission issue directly to a change of power, turning it from an institutional complaint into a fight to change the government.

It is also worth noting that Kharge did not mention his own state of Karnataka, or any Congress-ruled state. His entire focus was on the Centre, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra, that is, where the BJP or its allies are in power. This was the politics of the electoral target, and a clear signal of his strategy.
nazar: At this rally Kharge did what the opposition needed most: as Congress president he became the voice of the whole alliance. His language was aggressive, but he did not target any partner party. That was his greatest political sense.

Talk of digging someone out of the netherworld sounds sharp, but it will carry weight only if there is a solid process behind it. Otherwise it too will remain a slogan, and the government will get a chance to dismiss it as sentiment.
sawal: Will the talk of saving democracy remain limited to changing power, or will it also include reform of institutions?
ref: Governments of theft

This opposition slogan has become part of electoral language over the past few months. It means that power was won not by the people's votes but by tampering with the voter roll. The BJP calls it a baseless charge.
ank: states whose governments were called governments of theft

h: Mamata Banerjee: we did not lose, we were made to lose
dek: The former Bengal chief minister made the rally both emotional and sharp. She called the SIR a special relief for the BJP and asked Gen Z to take charge of the movement.
body: Mamata Banerjee came to the rally in the same open bus as Rahul Gandhi and Akhilesh Yadav. The first sentence she said on reaching the stage became the most emotional line of the day: we did not lose, we were made to lose. It was not only about election results; it was the beginning of the whole argument she was going to weave.

She said Bengal had been a victim of the SIR. According to her the chief election commissioner had removed more than one crore votes in Bengal, and that is why the Trinamool Congress did not lose the election but was made to lose. Mocking the SIR, she said its full name was Special Intensive Relief, given to the BJP. That was the sharpest jab in her speech.

Mamata said the BJP had looted the EVMs, looted democracy, looted the Constitution, looted people's rights and looted even the counting process. She alleged that Gyanesh Kumar had centralised the electoral system and hijacked it. Then she asked the CEC directly: Mr Gyanesh Kumar, when will you vanish?

She said this fight would be avenged through democracy, and the BJP would have to go. She called on party workers and leaders to stay united and said there should be no division on the basis of caste, religion, colour or community, because this fight belongs to everyone who believes in democracy and the Constitution.

At the rally she praised the struggle of the Cockroach Janta Party and Gen Z. She said I appeal to Gen Z, students, young people, the CJP and all democratic organisations to come together and take the movement forward. To the young she said: you have to take the command; we will show the way and give suggestions, but the future is yours.

Mamata also appealed to investigating agencies and the police not to work as puppets of the BJP, and asked the judiciary to play an active role in protecting democracy. At the end of her speech she sang out a nursery rhyme: vote theft, yes papa; democracy theft, yes papa; you looted, BJP papa. That jab was the clearest sample of her style, in which a serious charge is delivered in a light refrain.
nazar: Mamata turned Bengal's defeat into the rally's biggest emotional weapon. She did not say we lost on policy; she said straight out that we were made to lose. That language is a source of energy for her workers, but it is also true that calling every defeat theft can land you in difficulty later.

Her appeal to hand the command to Gen Z was her cleverest political move. It made her not just a leader of Bengal but the most experienced voice in opposition politics across the country, while keeping her connected to the youth movement.
sawal: Will calling Bengal's defeat a manufactured loss strengthen the movement, or will the claim weaken without evidence?
ref: Hijack
Mamata's charge is that the entire control of the electoral process is being run from Delhi, which is ending the rights of states and the role of the local commission.
ank: 1 crore+

h: Akhilesh Yadav: Ramlila Maidan is the Haldighati of democracy
dek: The Samajwadi Party chief tied the rally straight to 2027. He claimed 1.27 crore Hindu votes had been cut in Uttar Pradesh, and said those who came from UP would get their farewell from UP.
body: Akhilesh Yadav presented the clearest electoral arithmetic at the rally. He said that if 1.27 crore Hindu votes had been cut in Uttar Pradesh, then work out the math across 403 assembly constituencies: roughly thirty-one thousand votes less in each seat. He offered the number in reply to Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath's claim that more than one crore Hindu voters had been struck off in the SIR.

Akhilesh said the real point was not whose votes were cut and how many. The real point was that the BJP, seeing defeat, was putting the blame on others. According to him the BJP knows it cannot win among the people, and so it is using the Election Commission. He said those who claimed to have a foot as immovable as Angad's now know that there is no ground left to stand on.

He called Ramlila Maidan the Haldighati of democracy. The reference was clear: this is the place from where the next turn begins. He then said that those who once reached power in Delhi from Uttar Pradesh would get their farewell from Uttar Pradesh too. Pointing to the 2027 election, he said the farewell would be such that the BJP and its allies would not be able to return.

Akhilesh jabbed at the BJP's 'double engine' slogan with a reference to Kashi. He said those who claimed to run a double-engine government had been answered by the people of Kashi. The reference was aimed directly at the prime minister's parliamentary seat of Varanasi.

At the rally he also said questions should be raised about the use of the money collected for the Ram temple. His whole speech rested on the argument that the voter-roll issue is not merely an Election Commission mistake but a strategy of pinning the blame for the BJP's defeat on others.

Akhilesh's strategy was clear: he was using the rally as a national platform while preparing for the Uttar Pradesh election. By raising the cutting of Hindu votes he challenged the BJP's Hindutva argument on its own ground, and tried to show that the voter-roll problem belongs not to one community but to all.
nazar: Akhilesh connected this rally to his state's election more successfully than anyone else. He gave figures, did the math and spoke directly of 2027. That is the mark of his politics: even on a national stage he speaks the politics of his state.

Raising the cutting of Hindu votes was his biggest gamble, because it tries to plant doubt among the BJP's core voters. But it is also his most delicate gamble, because it needs solid numbers; otherwise it will remain only a political statement.
sawal: Will the 2027 election be fought on the voter roll, or will the issue not convert into votes?
ref: Haldighati
The battle of 1576 where Maharana Pratap's and Akbar's armies met. It is often used as a symbol of resistance, and of continuing the struggle even after defeat.

h: Tejashwi Yadav: today Ramlila hosts a Mahabharata, and Shakuni is rolling the dice
dek: The RJD leader began his speech like a story and arrived straight at software contracts. He asked who built the voter-roll software and where its documents are.
body: Tejashwi Yadav began his speech with a comparison. He said Ramlila Maidan is traditionally known for staging the Ramayana, but today a Mahabharata has been organised here against those who steal votes. He then recalled the story of the Mahabharata: Shakuni's dice, and the game that began not on a battlefield but in a court.

He said that same Shakuni is playing his game today, and that is why we are forced to fight. He did not use the metaphor only to decorate his speech but to say that tampering with the electoral process is not an ordinary glitch but a thought-out move.

Tejashwi then turned the speech towards concrete questions. He said the work on the voter-roll software had been given to a big company like TCS, and whether a tender was issued for it should be made public. He named Seema Khanna and asked what her role was in the whole system, and demanded that the documents be placed before the public. The question took the rally's charges beyond political statement to administrative accountability.

He said vote theft had begun in Bihar itself, and that the results there had proved elections can be changed through the voter roll. He called the government a number two government, and said constitutional institutions were working at the government's bidding instead of delivering justice.

Tejashwi demanded that Gyanesh Kumar be sent to jail. He also said all documents related to the voter roll and the counting should be made public so that people could see for themselves what had happened.
His speech was different in that he did not only make charges but asked for documents. That was his greatest strength, and it is also the opposition's greatest need: solid paper between the speeches.
nazar: Tejashwi used the Mahabharata metaphor best, because he made it not decoration but the language of accusation. Shakuni's dice became today's software and counting, and that is his political skill.

The questions about software and tenders are the most useful questions, because they can be answered with documents. If the opposition takes these questions to court and to the Right to Information, the movement can get the solid ground it is looking for.
sawal: Should the documents on the voter-roll software and the counting be made public so that every citizen can check for themselves?
ref: TCS
Tata Consultancy Services, one of the country's largest information technology companies. Tejashwi's question was about the contract for voter-roll software and its tender.
ank: demand: make the software and counting documents public

voice.name: Tejashwi Yadav

h: Dipankar Bhattacharya: this is a surgical strike on the right to vote
dek: The CPI(ML) Liberation general secretary called the SIR an attack on people's voting rights, compared Delhi's situation to military rule, and asked the young to join the movement.
body: Dipankar Bhattacharya spoke the clearest and harshest language on behalf of the Left parties at the rally. He said the whole country had understood that the SIR is a weapon to snatch people's right to vote, a surgical strike on the people by the government. The phrase surgical strike was chosen deliberately, because it is the government's own language, and it was turned around and aimed at the government.

He said that in a democracy the right to vote and the right to protest are both fundamental, and both are under attack. His charge was that the government was trying to suppress the movement, and that people were being stopped from gathering at Jantar Mantar. He said it felt as if military rule had been imposed in Delhi.

Bhattacharya called the crowd at Ramlila Maidan a historic moment and said the movement should now reach every state. He demanded that the 2023 law on the appointment of the chief election commissioner and election commissioners be changed, because that law weakens the autonomy of the commission.

Referring to Ambedkar, he said Ambedkar had given everyone the right to vote, and we will not let it be taken away. He appealed especially to the young and to Gen Z to join the movement and to make the voter-roll issue the main issue in the coming elections. He mentioned the elections in Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Uttarakhand.

The Left's strategy was visible at the rally: it sees the issue not merely as an Election Commission failure but as a question of the Constitution and democracy. Bhattacharya also said the fight was no longer of any one party but of everyone, and so it should take the shape of a people's movement.

The most important part of his speech was his demand on the 2023 law, because it was the first time a Left leader at the rally spoke not only of a resignation but of changing the law. That demand gives the movement a concrete policy goal that can outlast the crowd at a rally.
nazar: With the phrase surgical strike, Bhattacharya returned the government's own language to it. This is the sharpest weapon in political language, because it needs no new words for an accusation; you only have to turn the government's words around.

The demand on the 2023 law was the most useful part of his speech. A demand for a resignation rests on one person; a demand to change the law rests on an institution. If the opposition adopts this demand, the movement can get the lasting agenda it needs.
sawal: Can the demand to change the 2023 law on appointing election commissioners become the opposition's shared agenda?
ref: The 2023 law

The law on appointing the chief election commissioner and election commissioners, under which the selection committee has the prime minister, a Union minister and a leader of the opposition. Critics say the government's side weighs too heavy in it.
Surgical strike
The government used this phrase for a cross-border action in 2016. Bhattacharya turned it around to say the SIR is a surgical strike on people's right to vote.
ank: states where the issue will be raised in the next election

h: From Sukumar Sen to Gyanesh Kumar: where the Election Commission lost our trust
dek: JNU-educated Syed Mohammad Raghib argues that the Election Commission will win back its credibility not by denying charges but by putting its papers and data on the table.
body: Raghib begins with a Guardian report that spoke of nearly 130 million names being removed from voter lists. The question now, he says, is not how much power Article 324 gives the Commission, but whether people still trust the way that power is used.

The writer looks back. In 1951-52 Sukumar Sen ran the first election, with about 170 million voters and nearly two lakh (200,000) polling stations. T.N. Seshan gave the model code of conduct teeth. By 2024 the number of voters had grown to about 980 million. Raghib accepts that running elections on this scale is a real achievement, but scale is no answer to questions about transparency.

Then he turns to appointments. The 2023 law removed the Chief Justice from the selection committee and put in a minister chosen by the Prime Minister. For the writer, the real issue is not proving that any one person did wrong, but whether the system has a wall that protects it from pressure.

On the SIR he is careful. Names cut from the draft list are not, by themselves, proof of wrongful exclusion. But migrant workers, the elderly and poor people without papers may suffer the most. He does not treat the at least 14 objections raised by two commissioners as a failure either, as long as the full record is made public.

Finally the writer lists five reforms: open, criteria-based appointments; figures for names added and removed in every constituency; orders that give reasons; complaints under the code of conduct settled within a fixed time; and a technical audit. Citing criticism from three former election commissioners, he says the aim is not to weaken the Commission but to make it accountable.
nazar: This article is a calm voice amid the noise of slogans, and that is what makes it useful. With the streets demanding a resignation and the government calling every question a conspiracy, Raghib's insistence that the evidence be examined is in fact the toughest test for the Commission. How will an institution that hides the objections of its own commissioners pass that test?

Those whose names were cut are feared to be mostly migrants, Dalits, Adivasis (indigenous communities), Muslims and women living alone. For them, making every booth's figures public is not a technical reform. It is the first condition for saving their vote.
sawal: Why is the record of the fourteen objections being kept from the public?
ref: Article 324
The provision of the Constitution that gives the Election Commission full authority to hold elections, prepare voter lists and oversee them.
Sukumar Sen
India's first Chief Election Commissioner, who ran the first general election of 1951-52 with almost no precedent to go by.

h: A collapse of trust: the Election Commission falls from 51 to 28 per cent
dek: Singapore-based researcher Ronojoy Sen says that even if Gyanesh Kumar goes, it will take a long time for the Commission to regain its credibility.
body: In a short analysis, Ronojoy Sen of the Institute of South Asian Studies at the National University of Singapore tries to look at the Election Commission's current crisis from the outside. He notes that since the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) began in Bihar in June 2025, more than 130 million names have been removed from voter lists, and now the cracks inside the Commission have also come into view.

Citing media investigations, Sen says election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had recorded objections several times over ten months. The issues were registering new voters, deleting and restoring names, and oversight of the voter-list software. For four months before September, the three commissioners had not even held a full meeting.

The biggest dispute is over Form 6. In July 2026 a question was added asking whether the applicant, or their parents or grandparents, were on the list of the previous SIR, and it was not possible to proceed without answering. Joshi's view was that the form could not be changed without the government changing the rules. In West Bengal, the Commission appealed against 1.6 million people whom officers appointed by the court had found eligible.

Sen also recalls history. Until 1993 the Commission had a single commissioner. Then two more were added to rein in T.N. Seshan, so that the chief commissioner could not decide alone. The 2023 law tilted the selection committee in the government's favour.

According to the writer, the opposition does not have the numbers for impeachment, so the pressure is coming from the street, including from the young people's Cockroach Janta Party. Lokniti-CSDS surveys show that those who fully trusted the Commission fell from 51 per cent in 2019 to 28 per cent in 2024.
nazar: This analysis shows that the crisis is bigger than any one officer. When the body that makes the rules ignores objections from its own members and puts the burden of proof on the voter, the first to be left out are those without papers: migrant workers, Dalit and Adivasi settlements, women who move home after marriage, and Muslims who are kept under suspicion.
To restore trust, the structure must change more than the face, especially the way appointments are made.
sawal: How does a new voter get registered by being asked for their grandparents' names?
ref: Form 6
The application form for becoming a new voter. It is alleged that in July 2026 a question about ancestors on the list was added without changing the rules.
Lokniti-CSDS
A Delhi research institute that surveys voters' leanings and their trust in institutions during elections.
