h: Karnataka's voter list: Bengaluru, women and young people hit hardest
dek: According to an early analysis by the Sabar Institute, nearly a fifth of the state's voters were left out of the draft list in the SIR.
body: The Special Intensive Revision of Karnataka's voter list began on 20 June, and the final list was published on 27 October. The Sabar Institute compared the draft lists with the 2023 and 2018 election results, the 2011 Census and district income data. The final list is about 9.9 million names shorter than before.

Bengaluru took the biggest blow. Less than 20 per cent of the state's voters live there, but about 45 per cent of all deletions came from the city. Every seat in the city lost at least 36 per cent of its voters. In five seats, including Bommanahalli, CV Raman Nagar and BTM Layout, more names were cut than the number of people who even voted in 2023.

Leave aside names removed because of death, and women appear to be more affected. Among those aged 18 to 29, two women were cut for every man. In Uttara Kannada, 70 per cent of living voters deleted were women.

The report says voters with Muslim names make up 14.4 per cent of all deletions, close to their share of the population. But they were 1.76 times more likely to be marked as 'registered elsewhere' rather than dead. Districts with a larger Scheduled Caste population also saw more deletions. In 145 of the 224 seats, the number of living voters removed is larger than the previous winning margin. The institute says clearly that this is not proof of targeting, but a pointer to where audits should be done.
nazar: When more names are cut in a seat than the winning margin, it is no longer just a matter of administrative clean-up. The burden falls on people who move cities looking for work, on women who move home after marriage, and on settlements with more Dalits. That shows paper checks weed out the poor and the weak first. The demand for an independent audit can no longer be put off.
sawal: If more names are cut than the winning margin, whose mandate is it?
ref: Special Intensive Revision (SIR)
The Election Commission's drive in which the voter list is prepared afresh and every voter is made to fill in an enumeration form.
Sabar Institute
A research organisation that released this early report on Karnataka's draft lists.

h: An affidavit arrives, but the fog stays: half answers on Form 6
dek: A Navbharat editorial says the Election Commission's reply in the Supreme Court does not give a full picture of the SIR or of the declaration added to Form 6.
body: The INDIA alliance filed a petition in the Supreme Court questioning irregularities in the SIR and the conduct of the Election Commission. The Commission filed an affidavit fully defending its work. The Navbharat editorial feels the reply cleared up some things, but many key questions remain where they were. About 130 million people's names were cut from voter lists in the SIR, so the matter was already very sensitive.

The dispute deepened when news came that election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had objected 14 times to decisions of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The Commission says all SIR decisions were unanimous and no disagreement can be linked to those decisions.

The real tangle is the extra declaration added to Form 6, which asked a new voter to state that their parents were voters in 2002. The Commission calls it a separate document. The editorial asks: if it really was separate, how were lakhs (hundreds of thousands) of applications submitted without ticking it? It finds the explanation that the portal's design caused confusion hard to understand. The two dissenting commissioners had asked the same thing: was this condition added at the level of a programmer or of the Commission?

According to the editorial, even if the decision was unanimous, the petitioners' objection stands: the power to change the form lies with the Law Ministry, and changing rules approved by Parliament is going beyond the Commission's remit. An internal work-allocation order of 28 July is also under question. It allegedly gave the Chief Election Commissioner special power to decide alone, and was not implemented after the other two commissioners objected.
The conclusion is that the court can call for the necessary papers, and until the layers of the Commission's decision-making are opened up, its explanation will remain incomplete.
nazar: This unease comes not from an opposition paper but from a mainstream Hindi newspaper, and that is what makes it important. The question is no longer about a slogan. It is about a tick-box that asked a new voter to account for their parents in 2002.

Such a condition weighs first on those whose families were working somewhere else that year, or who never had papers at all: migrants, Dalits, Adivasis, Muslims and poor women. The court must make sure that a citizenship check does not slip into the voter list through the back door.
sawal: If lakhs of applications went through without the tick, whose condition was it?
ref: Form 6
The application to register a new name on the voter list. The Supreme Court is hearing a case on the declaration about parents in 2002 that was added to it.
SIR
Special Intensive Revision, in which the voter list is made almost from scratch. The Commission says dead, duplicate and moved-away voters were removed in it.

h: Kerala's probe will not touch Gyanesh Kumar
dek: Vinod Mathew says the Kerala government's vigilance inquiry is more noise than impact, and the real fight is on the streets of Delhi.
body: Senior journalist Vinod Mathew describes what happened in Delhi on 10 October as an exercise to save one man. According to him, trains coming to the capital were stopped, 45 metro stations were shut, the internet was cut and heavy police forces were deployed. The target is Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of having crores (tens of millions) of names cut through the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter lists.

In this climate, Kerala's home minister Ramesh Chennithala ordered a vigilance inquiry against Gyanesh Kumar. The case goes back to 2006, when he was secretary of the Public Works Department in Kerala. Payments for the PATI-BEL project, linked to a Malaysian company, had been stopped, and its manager Lee Si Bean took his own life. There was a rumour that the suicide note named Gyanesh Kumar, but the preliminary inquiry at the time found no such evidence.

The writer says there is no hope of a verified note turning up twenty years later, so the probe is like chasing a ghost. He recalls that after moving to the Defence Ministry in 2006, Gyanesh Kumar never returned to Kerala. He retired as Cooperation Secretary in January 2024, became an election commissioner within weeks, and then Chief Election Commissioner in February 2025.

Mathew links the story to a wider trend, where retiring judges and officers move close to power. He lists several former judges and bureaucrats, and repeats former chief secretary G.G. Thomson's claim that Gyanesh Kumar had suggested the same path to him too.
According to the writer, the Kerala government really wants to be seen standing with the youth movement. But as long as Gyanesh Kumar stays in his chair, the ground under this probe will remain weak.
nazar: This article is a needed warning that tangling the fight for the right to vote in old, hazy cases can weaken the movement. The real question is the names cut in the SIR, most of them belonging to the poor, migrant workers, women and minorities.
Instead of showy inquiries, state governments should demand an account of every name cut in their own states.
sawal: How will a twenty-year-old suicide note win today's fight?
ref: SIR
The Special Intensive Revision of voter lists, in which every voter must prove their eligibility again. It is alleged that names were cut on a large scale.
Vigilance inquiry
The state's anti-corruption bureau examines an officer's conduct. A case is made only after the preliminary inquiry.

h: Having to take to the streets is a failure of democracy
dek: Young people's anger over the voter lists shows that between elections, citizens have no reliable way left to make themselves heard.
body: Over the past few weeks, young people across the country have been raising questions about irregularities in the revision of voter lists and about how exams are run, through petitions, social media campaigns and street protests. According to the two writers, who are associated with the organisation Janaagraha, this anger is not about one issue. The real complaint is that after voting once in five years, ordinary people have no solid way to hold their elected representatives to account.

The writers recall Ambedkar's famous 1949 speech, in which he said that when constitutional methods are open, there is no need for satyagraha (non-violent resistance) and civil disobedience. They argue that 75 years later, for most people these constitutional paths either do not exist or are so costly and tiring that people treat the street as the last court.

Whether it is drinking water, schools, hospitals, broken roads or recruitment exams, citizens make rounds of offices from the panchayat (village council) to the Centre. The writers say this structure is inherited from British rule, in which the government is the giver and the citizen merely the receiver.

They see the cure in three changes. First, forums in the gram sabha (village assembly), ward committee and the constituencies of MLAs and MPs where people are heard before decisions are made. Second, it should be visible to everyone, in a simple form, where budget and scheme money went. Third, governments should give an account every quarter and every year, and take responsibility for failures.

The writers say the country must move away from a model in which you have to knock on the doors of the High Court and Supreme Court for every basic right. The government should listen before people have to shout.
nazar: The article does not name the Election Commission, but the context is clear. When the right to vote itself hangs on a form and an office decision, the deafness of the bodies meant to hear complaints hurts most those who have no papers, time or lawyers: migrant workers, Dalit and Adivasi settlements, women who move home after marriage.

But there is a gap too. Forums for participation are good, but the current movement is asking for accountability, not consultation. Where an institution is accused of cutting names, what is needed is an independent inquiry and open records, more than a ward committee.
sawal: After voting, where does a citizen take their complaint?
ref: Janaagraha
A Bengaluru non-governmental organisation that works on urban governance and citizen participation.
Grammar of Anarchy
Ambedkar's speech in the Constituent Assembly on 25 November 1949, in which he spoke of avoiding the methods of agitation when constitutional paths are available.

h: A flurry of reforms: admitting mistakes, or answering after being caught?
dek: An analysis by Aaj Tak's Dhirendra Rai says the Election Commission's seven new reforms have become a fresh weapon for the opposition, and the government is caught in a dilemma over Gyanesh Kumar.
body: On the streets of Delhi, the Congress, the Aam Aadmi Party and the Cockroach Janta Party are demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Dhirendra Rai writes that amid this noise, the Commission is quietly working on two fronts: adding new voters through Form 6, and quickly changing rules in response to criticism. The Supreme Court has sent notices to the government, the Commission and Gyanesh Kumar himself, asking for a clear answer on the changes to the voter list.

The spark was an Indian Express report saying the Chief Election Commissioner had overridden dozens of objections from the other two commissioners. In reply, the Commission called the disagreement normal, said the decisions were unanimous and promised to publish meeting agendas in advance.

Then came seven reforms for the revision that began in 17 states from 15 October. Parties will get readable PDF lists instead of blurry scanned copies; there will be a separate list of names added and removed; one person will not be able to file more than ten Form 7 applications to have names removed; BLOs (booth-level officers) will check by visiting homes; and experts from the IITs will audit the Commission's software, including ECINet. The opposition argues that these reforms themselves admit the earlier process was hasty and full of flaws.

The second part of the piece is about the government's dilemma. When BJP ministers defend the Commission, it confirms the charge that the Commission has been captured. The Chief Election Commissioner holds a constitutional post and can be removed only by impeachment in Parliament, and the government has no reason to do so, while the opposition does not have the numbers.

Rai concludes that the government can neither fully defend the Commission nor shake off the charges, while the opposition can keep up the pressure by calling every result a collusion between the government and the Commission. The writer also says the charge that more minority names were cut is not proved by the data, though he does not give details.
nazar: This analysis from a big TV group has no sympathy for the movement, yet its own list gives weight to the charges. If a limit now has to be put on how many deletion applications one person can file, who was this door open for before? This is exactly the opposition's charge: that such bulk objections hit Muslims, Dalits and migrant workers.
The claim that the data does not prove the charges is also made without data. An inquiry can only be answered by an inquiry, and the IIT audit will matter only if its report is made public.
sawal: Before the ten-application limit, how many people had thousands of names cut?
ref: Form 7
The application to have someone's name removed from the voter list or to object to it. It is alleged that it was used in bulk to get genuine voters' names cut.
Removing the Chief Election Commissioner
Under Article 324 of the Constitution, the CEC can be removed only like a Supreme Court judge, by a motion passed by a special majority in both houses of Parliament.

h: A Gulf peace pact amid war: not by keeping Iran out
dek: Abdullah Baabood argues that amid the US-Israeli war on Iran, only a non-aggression pact among all eight Gulf coastal countries can save the region.
body: In a recent speech in Cambridge, Oman's foreign minister Badr Al-Busaidi proposed a 'non-aggression' pact among all eight Gulf coastal countries: the six members of the Gulf Cooperation Council, Iraq and Iran. Abdullah Baabood accepts that this may seem hasty while a war is on, but says such pacts are most useful exactly when trust is lowest.

The writer recalls that in November 1976 these eight countries sat at one table in Muscat, and that was the last time. Then the Iranian revolution, Soviet troops in Afghanistan and the Iran-Iraq war split the region into blocs built on keeping each other out. His argument is simple: Iran holds almost half of the Gulf's coast, so no security structure can last without it.

The idea is not new. In 2019 Iran made such an offer, which its Arab neighbours rejected. But this year's war has changed the mood. According to the writer, Saudi Arabia and Qatar too are now talking of similar talks with Iran.

Baabood does not dismiss the Arab neighbours' suspicion of Iran. After drone attacks on Oman's Musandam and Al Wusta in July, Muscat itself lodged a formal complaint with Tehran. So instead of words about trust, he wants binding conditions: no use of force, no interference in internal affairs, no attacks on power stations and water desalination plants, no support for armed groups across borders.

The start should be small: military hotlines, rules for encounters at sea, and temporary arrangements for shipping through Hormuz. The writer accepts that the US and Israel will stay outside this framework, but says it would be a big step even to settle that differences give no one the right to crush a neighbour's security.
nazar: The price of Hormuz being closed is being paid by Indian kitchens and by the lives of millions of Indian workers in the Gulf. The Gulf order that leaned on outside powers has been thrown into the fire again and again, so the countries of the region sitting down together is the most practical way forward. Delhi too should be a voice for peace here, not a spectator.
sawal: When will the Muscat table of fifty years ago be laid again?
ref: Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC)
A body formed in 1981 by Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman. Iran and Iraq are not members.
Hormuz Peace Endeavour (HOPE)
A proposal put to the United Nations in 2019 by Iran's President Rouhani, suggesting a peace pact among the countries on the Hormuz coast.

h: Manusmriti in judgments: a judge's pen is bound by the Constitution
dek: Listing references to scriptures in several recent court judgments, Venkat P.S. Vemuri says ancient texts can neither create crimes nor decide a woman's household duties.
body: On 26 October a sessions court in Gujarat sentenced three people to life imprisonment in a cow-slaughter case. The 76-page judgment explained the religious importance of the cow by citing the Manusmriti (an ancient Hindu law text) and the Vedas. Four days earlier, while hearing a wife's plea for maintenance, the Allahabad High Court quoted the Manusmriti verse that speaks of supporting aged parents, a wife and a child.

Vemuri says both judgments actually rested on law, not scripture. The Gujarat judgment stood on the 1954 animal preservation law and Article 48 of the Constitution, and in Allahabad the husband's duty had already been settled by a 2022 Supreme Court judgment. In the writer's view, a duty that the law has already fixed does not need Manu's seal.

The danger shows when the citation goes beyond decoration and starts to change the outcome. In 2024 the Jharkhand High Court, citing the Vedas and the Manusmriti, held that a wife who left without caring for her parents-in-law could not get maintenance for herself. Courts in Karnataka, Odisha and Madurai have also brought the Gita and Sanskrit verses into judgments.

The writer recalls old precedents. The Manusmriti is not part of the Constitution and never became law. In 1955-56 Parliament ended the era of the smritis (traditional law texts) by passing the Hindu laws on marriage, succession and adoption. In 1979 and 1980 the Supreme Court itself held that where custom has changed, what a text says carries no legal weight.

Citing judgments such as Navtej Johar and Joseph Shine, Vemuri says the court has itself struck down laws built on patriarchy. Judges may read texts to understand history, but a citizen's rights and duties will be decided only by the Constitution and the laws made by Parliament.
nazar: If the text that Ambedkar publicly burned returns in the language of the courts, the rights of Dalits and women are the first to be put at stake. If a single verse can make a woman's maintenance depend on serving her in-laws, the promise of equality stays on paper. The judiciary itself should draw this line clearly.
sawal: How did one verse take away a wife's maintenance in Jharkhand?
ref: Article 48
A Directive Principle of the Constitution that asks the state to improve farming and animal husbandry and to try to stop the slaughter of cows and calves. It cannot be directly enforced in court.
Narasu Appa Mali judgment (1951)
A Bombay High Court judgment that held uncodified personal law to be outside the test of fundamental rights. It is still debated today.

h: Niyamgiri in the crosshairs again: bauxite, weapons and Adivasis
dek: Felix Padel and Malvika Gupta argue that Vedanta's new attempt to mine Niyamgiri is part of a bigger plan to sell Odisha's minerals into the market of global wars.
body: On 26 September, Vedanta chairman Anil Agarwal met Odisha Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi and promised an investment of one lakh crore rupees (1 trillion rupees), a hospital and lakhs of jobs. In return he asked for quick approval for bauxite mining in Niyamgiri. This is the same Niyamgiri that gram sabhas (village assemblies), held on the Supreme Court's direction in 2013, had saved from mining. The two writers, both anthropologists, note that this meeting came after the arrest of Niyamgiri movement leaders Lada Sikaka and Lingaraj Azad.

According to the writers, since 2023 the police have been cracking down on Adivasis and Dalits opposing mining in the nearby Sijimali, Kutrumali and Khandualmali hills. It is alleged that public hearings were held under pressure, villages were attacked, and people such as doctor Randall Sequeira and Dalit leader Laxman Nayak were sent to jail.

The article places this on a bigger map. During the Chief Minister's UAE visit in September, deals worth about 25 billion dollars were made linked to Adani's mines and a new smelter. Odisha has been made a 'rare earth corridor', and an India-US minerals agreement has also been signed. The writers recall that in April Agarwal argued for private arms factories to profit from the wars in West Asia, and aluminium is the basic metal of the arms industry.

Padel and Gupta also question the slogan of 'green transition', in whose name mining is growing rather than shrinking. For them, the Kondh Adivasis' bond with the hills is not sentimentality: these hills are the home of their god Niyam Raja, and year-round streams flow from here.

The writers give the examples of Ecuador and New Zealand, where rivers and mountains have been given legal rights, and say mining must become an issue in national politics. Otherwise the displacement of Adivasis will turn into a kind of cultural wiping out.
nazar: Niyamgiri's 2013 gram sabhas show that an Adivasi 'no' can also be a legal decision. If that 'no' is made meaningless again before big investment figures, PESA and the Forest Rights Act will remain only in books. The issue is no longer only Odisha's. It is also about whose wars India's minerals are being dug up for.
sawal: Which war front will the metal from Niyam Raja's hills finally reach?
ref: Niyamgiri gram sabhas (2013)
On the Supreme Court's order, 12 gram sabhas in Odisha rejected Vedanta's mining. It is seen as a landmark example of Adivasi consent.
Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC)
The international principle that before a project in an indigenous area, the community there must give its consent, free of pressure and with full information.

h: Pakistan's media in the shadow of death, and now an 'MI6' label on top
dek: Hamid Mir writes that journalists in Pakistan are worse off than in Musharraf's time, and those who ask questions are now being branded foreign agents with a fake document.
body: Senior journalist Mazhar Abbas's book 'Media Under the Shadow of Death' was launched in Islamabad. Its host, anchor Absa Komal, had been fired shortly before for raising the issue of journalists working without pay outside the press club. Hamid Mir says losing jobs and being taken off screen are everyday matters, but when an experienced journalist says the media is close to dying, it is a serious warning.

Mir recalls that in 2012 he and some colleagues petitioned the Supreme Court to shut the information ministry's secret fund and to hold to account those who bribed journalists. After more than a hundred hearings, only the secret fund was stopped. A code of conduct was made but never enforced. Among those colleagues was Arshad Sharif, who was killed in Kenya while in exile.

The writer says that in Musharraf's time five anchors were banned for a few months; today 15 anchors are missing from the screen. At a meeting in Lahore, journalists from the provinces described the situation: offices are closing in Balochistan, protests are banned outside the Karachi Press Club, 60 per cent of journalists in Punjab are unemployed, 30 journalists have been killed in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa since 9/11, and Gilgit-Baltistan has no internet at all.

Journalists' unions called the 2025 PECA law a 'black law' and announced they would take to the streets. The very next day an alleged MI6 document spread on social media, calling the meeting's organisers, including Mir, pawns of the British intelligence agency. The writer calls it forged.

Mir remarks wryly that all his assets are listed in his tax returns, and that the rulers should read Jinnah's speeches on press freedom. If some foreign agency really wanted to save the media, he says, he would thank it too.
nazar: On this side of the border too, branding a questioning journalist with a 'foreign hand', removing anchors overnight and scaring people with IT laws is a familiar method. Hamid Mir's story is a mirror: when the media is choked, the first news to disappear is from small towns, minorities and workers.
sawal: From five anchors to fifteen: which government will the ban count be recorded against?
ref: PECA
Pakistan's Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act. Since the 2025 amendment, cases against journalists in the name of 'fake news' have increased.
Arshad Sharif
A Pakistani journalist who was killed by police gunfire in Kenya in October 2022 after leaving the country. Questions remain about the investigation into his death.

h: France is not 'burning'; its injustice is smouldering
dek: Historian Ludivine Bantigny says headlines fixed on the damage in France's student movement hide the violence that happens every day through inequality and repression.
body: For weeks, media around the world have been showing burning buildings and smashed shops in France, with headlines like 'France is burning'. Ludivine Bantigny reminds us that this movement is mostly peaceful and the students are asking for better schools and colleges. Her complaint is that everything is crammed into the word 'violence': a shop window, a burnt car, protesters injured by police, and shots fired at an unarmed crowd.

This mixing makes damage to property and an attack on a person look equal, and puts protest and its repression on the same scale. The writer draws on Brazilian archbishop Dom Hélder Câmara, who named three forms of violence: oppressive injustice, the revolt it gives rise to, and then repression. Bantigny adds a fourth: the violence of inequality, discrimination and humiliation that goes on even in a society that looks calm.

Then she opens up France's history. The Bastille, peasants burning feudal records, the Paris Commune, the official killed at the Decazeville mine, the barricades of May 1968, the steelworkers of 1979, the Yellow Vests, and the anger that flared after young people died at police hands in 2005 and 2023. Each time, there was a concrete injustice behind the anger.

According to the writer, vandalism is often a political language, aimed at symbols of power that seem deaf. The most dramatic acts are usually done by a small section, and they are not the identity of the whole movement.
Her conclusion is that saying violence suddenly broke out in a peaceful France is a misreading of the country's political and social history.
nazar: The same lens is used in India too: one burnt bus is made the face of an entire movement, while detention, police batons and daily evictions are called 'law and order'. To understand the anger of Dalits, Adivasis and workers, we must first count the silent violence done to them every day.
sawal: A burnt car and a lost eye: are both the same 'violence'?
ref: Paris Commune (1871)
The self-governing government set up by Paris workers after the defeat by Prussia, crushed by the army in the 'Bloody Week' with thousands killed.
Dom Hélder Câmara
Brazilian archbishop and a major figure in liberation theology, who called poverty itself the 'first violence'.

h: Patel and Nehru: many quarrels, but always together
dek: On Patel's 151st birth anniversary, Ramachandra Guha uses the new edition of Rajmohan Gandhi's Patel biography to argue that setting Patel against Nehru is a betrayal of history.
body: Rajmohan Gandhi's book 'Patel: A Life' came out in 1991. In its introduction he wrote that free India got its legitimacy from three people, Gandhi, Nehru and Patel, but the country gave credit to Nehru generously, to Gandhi as a ritual and to Patel stingily. Thirty-five years later the book is back in a new edition, and according to Ramachandra Guha the climate has turned upside down: since 2014 the government has kept praising Patel and running down Nehru.

Guha praises the book for resting on Patel's letters, the diaries of his daughter Maniben, government records and old newspapers. Patel came from a farming family and was proud of his rural roots, and in the 1928 Bardoli Satyagraha his blunt, country speech brought the farmers together.

Patel's relationship with Gandhi was like devotion. During 16 months in jail in the 1930s, he would prepare a neem twig toothbrush for Gandhi every day, make him lemon water and copy out his letters. His differences with Nehru were real, but the two agreed on two things: freedom first, and nothing would work without Gandhi.

After Gandhi's assassination, Nehru wrote to Patel that the old quarrels were now meaningless and the two had to work together. Patel replied that he felt the same. On Nehru's birthday in 1948, Patel wrote that Gandhi had chosen Nehru as his rightful heir. Guha counts these letters among the most moving ever written between political colleagues.

In the introduction to the new edition, Rajmohan Gandhi says it is painful to see Patel used in a politics of Hindu supremacy and of keeping Muslims second-class, and that the Patel-versus-Nehru quarrel is an easy way to distract from real challenges.
nazar: The taller Patel's statue was built, the smaller his actual politics was made to look. Turning a leader who kept holding his colleague's hand even after disagreements into a flag for divisive politics is like putting history's seal on hatred against Muslims. Unity alongside disagreement: that is Patel's most useful legacy for India today.
sawal: Whose hero is the Patel who made neem toothbrushes in jail?
ref: Bardoli Satyagraha (1928)
A farmers' movement in Bardoli, Gujarat, against a rise in land revenue. After leading it, Vallabhbhai came to be called 'Sardar' (leader).
Rajmohan Gandhi
Historian and grandson of Mahatma Gandhi, who has written biographies of Gandhi, Patel, Rajaji and Ghaffar Khan.

h: House arrests and cases for those seeking justice for Sahil Wakode
dek: Activists who spoke up over the death of a Dalit student at IIT Bombay accuse the Mumbai police of repeatedly detaining them and confining them to their homes.
body: Sahil Wakode, a 20-year-old student at IIT Bombay, died by suicide. The institute first linked it to cheating in an exam, then withdrew the statement after protests. Professor Suryanarayana Doola is accused of abetment and caste discrimination, and an FIR has been registered against him under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act. He was removed as dean but remains in his job.

Now those seeking justice say the police are closing in on them instead. Deepali Salve, general secretary of the All India Independent Scheduled Castes Association, says she was put under house arrest three times. Even though permission had been given for a silent march at Chaityabhoomi, a case of unlawful assembly was filed against her and 12 others.

Samaya Korde, president of the Maharashtra Progressive Students Union, says police sit outside her house for eight or nine hours. Aamir Qazi of the AISF says he has been detained nine or ten times and now walks with a stick. People were packed into buses from Chaityabhoomi and taken to Tardeo police station, where candles and photos of Sahil were seized.

Sahil's parents are on a sit-in at Azad Maidan, where permission is not given on Saturdays and Sundays and on other days they must leave by 6 pm. The movement's demands are: removal of director Shireesh Kedare, making the institute's internal inquiry report public, Doola's suspension, and a Rohith Vemula Act. The Wire sent questions to the police but got no reply.
nazar: Treating those who ask questions about a Dalit student's death like criminals shows whom those in power want to protect. Seizing candles at Ambedkar's Chaityabhoomi is not just a matter of law and order. It is an insult. Until a binding law against caste discrimination on campuses is made, such deaths will keep getting lost in inquiry files.
sawal: Who gave the order to seize candles at Chaityabhoomi?
ref: Chaityabhoomi
Dr Ambedkar's memorial in Dadar, Mumbai, one of the most important places for the Dalit movement.
Rohith Vemula Act
A proposed law to stop caste discrimination in higher education institutions, demanded since Rohith Vemula's death in 2016.

h: Journalists attacked at Pulivendula booths, cameras smashed
dek: In Andhra Pradesh's civic polls, reporters were beaten and chased out of booths, and Jagan has demanded a fresh vote.
body: Voting for urban local bodies in Andhra Pradesh began at seven on Sunday morning, and reports of clashes soon came in from Pulivendula, former chief minister Jagan Mohan Reddy's home turf. India Today's Basheer and cameraman Vijay, and NTV's Suresh, were attacked while covering the polls, and their cameras were smashed.

A few minutes after the attack on Suresh, two News Minute reporters reached the booth at YSVRM Junior College. A group of men in white shirts stopped them from filming, told them things were not right and that they should leave. Then the police too asked them to go, 'to avoid trouble'. According to the report, TDP supporters appeared to have taken over the booth.

Jagan, who came to vote, alleged that YSRCP agents had been driven out of 70 of Pulivendula's 80 booths, that TDP workers had been camped at the booths since four in the morning, and that the police were helping them. He listed similar complaints from places such as Kadapa, Macherla, Tadipatri and Madanapalle, and demanded a repoll. There is also an allegation that a woman polling agent's arm was broken.

The TDP blamed the YSRCP for the violence and complained to the State Election Commission. TDP MLA Varla Ramaiah alleged that YSRCP men attacked the India Today cameraman. By one in the afternoon, turnout stood at 37.13 per cent across the state and 51.51 per cent in Pulivendula.
nazar: A camera at a booth is there so that wrongdoing gets recorded. When journalists are beaten and driven away, and the police too say 'leave', the first person left alone is the ordinary voter, who has no witness against fear. An inquiry should decide which party is to blame, but this open bullying in a local election hollows out the lowest rung of democracy.
sawal: At a booth where cameras are banned, whose hands hold the vote?
ref: Pulivendula
A town and assembly seat in Kadapa district, seen for decades as the stronghold of Y.S. Rajasekhara Reddy's family.
State Election Commission
The constitutional body that runs elections to municipal bodies and panchayats. It is separate from the Election Commission of India.

h: Madras High Court tells police not to allow protests targeting judges
dek: The court gave the direction after protests against a ruling on reservation for people who converted to Islam.
body: On Friday the Madras High Court told the Tamil Nadu police not to permit any protest or procession that personally targets a judge. If a permitted gathering turns into a personal attack on a judge, it should be ended at once and legal action taken. The order came on a public interest petition, which the court then closed.

The case goes back to a ruling of 25 June. It said that if a person from a backward, most backward or denotified community, or from a Scheduled Caste, embraces Islam, they cannot claim reservation in the Backward Class (Muslim) category. The Supreme Court upheld that ruling on 15 October.

The petitioner alleged that groups such as the Tamil Nadu Thowheed Jamath and the Tamil Nadu Muslim Munnetra Kazhagam then held protests across the state in which one judge of the bench that gave the ruling was personally targeted. Insulting and casteist remarks were allegedly made in posters, rallies and social media videos.

The court turned down a demand for a blanket ban on public discussion of court rulings or peaceful gatherings, saying that would go too far. The police and district administration must consider each application on its own. The court said citizens have every right to disagree with a ruling, but organised attacks on judges do not get the shield of free speech. The report does not carry the side of the organisations or the government.
nazar: It is good that the right to criticise a ruling survives, but leaving it to the police to decide what counts as 'personal targeting' is dangerous. Tamil Nadu already has complaints of a heavy hand on protests. The real issue is that Dalits and backward-caste people lose their reservation when they change their religion. Instead of pushing this debate off the streets, it should be allowed to happen openly in Parliament and in society.
sawal: Why does the measure of backwardness change the moment someone changes religion?
ref: Backward Class (Muslim) reservation
A separate share kept within Tamil Nadu's backward class quota for the backward sections among Muslims.
Public interest petition
A petition filed in court on a wide public question rather than a personal interest.

h: After Cyclone Arnab, south Odisha villages are cut off by water
dek: Thousands are homeless in Ganjam, Gajapati and Kandhamal, and rations are being flown by helicopter to villages that have been cut off.
body: Cyclone Arnab, which struck on 28 October, brought extraordinary rain to south Odisha. Rivers such as the Rushikulya and the Mahendratanaya burst their banks, and floods and landslides washed away roads and bridges. Villages in seven districts, Ganjam, Gajapati, Kandhamal, Koraput, Malkangiri, Nabarangpur and Rayagada, were surrounded by water.

According to the weather department, Patrapur in Ganjam recorded 546 millimetres of rain and Soroda 503 millimetres. About 42,500 people in 299 villages across 22 blocks of Ganjam were affected, and 11,882 were moved to safety. In Gajapati, about 20,000 people in 711 villages are affected, and 17,441 have been evacuated.

Teams from the NDRF, ODRAF and the fire service are taking people to flood and cyclone shelters, but strong currents have so far made it impossible to reach some of the worst-hit areas. Food was dropped by helicopter to villages that are cut off. After water was released from the Ghodahada dam, a warning went out that about a hundred crocodiles from the river could be swept into settlements.

The weather department has classed Arnab as a very severe cyclonic storm. Weather websites showed another low-pressure system alongside it, which may have strengthened the storm, but the department has not confirmed this. A new system forming over the Andaman Sea threatens more heavy rain in coastal Andhra.
nazar: In districts like Ganjam and Gajapati, a large part of the population is Adivasi (indigenous) people and small farmers, whose crops and mud houses can be swept away in one night. Odisha has learnt how to save lives in a cyclone, but the recovery after the flood goes down, the compensation and the repair of bridges and roads, often drags on for months. As the weather changes its ways, the scale of preparation must change too.
sawal: After 546 millimetres of rain, how many days will compensation take to arrive?
ref: Very severe cyclonic storm
A weather department category in which wind speeds are between 118 and 165 kilometres per hour.
ODRAF
Odisha Disaster Rapid Action Force, the state's own disaster relief force, set up in 2001.

h: Years on contract for Kasturba school teachers amounts to forced labour: High Court
dek: The Allahabad High Court has told the UP government to create posts within four months and, until then, pay every teacher Rs 17,000 a month.
body: The Lucknow bench of the Allahabad High Court has said that keeping teachers of Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalayas on low-paid contracts for years is like the begar (forced, unpaid labour) banned by Article 23 of the Constitution. Justice Pankaj Bhatia gave the ruling on 29 October on Archana Bauddh's petition and connected petitions. One petition included 376 other teachers along with Rita Verma.

These schools have run since 2004 and give girls from poor, deprived communities a place to live and study. The court heard that many teachers have taught for more than 15 years, yet each year they get a contract of 11 months and 29 days, then a one-day break, then a fresh contract.

The state argued that there are no sanctioned posts and that the scheme runs on shared money from the Centre and the state. The court did not accept this. It said that in a scheme running for more than twenty years, the work of teaching is permanent, and under the Right to Education Act it is the state's duty to provide teachers. The court also said that leaving girls from weaker sections in the hands of insecure, low-paid teachers is discrimination against those girls too.

Under the order, the government must create posts within four months, set service conditions like those of regular teachers, and consider regularisation on the basis of qualification and service. Until then, all Kasturba teachers in the state will get Rs 17,000 a month. The state cannot hold back payment on the ground that the Centre's money has not come.
nazar: This ruling is not only about pay. For years governments have run permanent work such as education, health and anganwadis (village childcare centres) on contracts and honorariums, and the burden falls mostly on women. The court has said plainly that calling permanent work temporary to get cheap labour is forced labour.

Now we will see whether the UP government creates the posts in four months or takes the path of appeal. The education of Dalit, Adivasi and poor girls rests on the very teachers who were themselves given no security.
sawal: Whose savings was the one-day break each year meant for?
ref: Article 23

This article of the Constitution bans begar and forced labour.
The Supreme Court has held that making people work for less than the minimum wage also falls within it.
Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalaya

A central scheme started in 2004 that runs residential schools for girls from deprived communities.
It is now part of the Samagra Shiksha Abhiyan.

h: A hive in the wall: Kumaon's women are saving the mountain bee
dek: In Uttarakhand's villages, hives built inside walls are disappearing, and the work of saving the native bee falls on the women left behind after the men migrated.
body: In the villages of Pithoragarh district, a square hollow used to be built into the thick mud walls of old houses, with a round opening to the outside. The native mountain bee, Apis cerana indica, makes its hive in it. A small door at the back stays sealed with mud and cow dung and is opened only to take out honey. This arrangement is now vanishing fast.

According to the report, these hives are mostly tended by women. When the men went to the cities for work, the women took over plastering the hollows, calling back stray swarms with a streak of honey, and feeding the bees ground amaranth or hemp seed in winter. Kumaon University biologist Nagma Parveen says that if this bee survives in Uttarakhand today, it is because of these women.

But new cement and brick houses have no room for wall hives. A 2013 study of the Gairsain block in Chamoli found that houses built before 1980 had on average more than 11 hives each, while those built between 2001 and 2010 had less than one. Of the 210 hives found in ten villages, not one was in a concrete house. In Kanta Devi's new house in Ramni village, the mason built the hollow so high that neither she nor the bees can reach it.

The weather is another blow. After heavy rain and storms this year, Shakuntala Devi's hives lie empty. Eighty-year-old Saraswati Devi remembers that one hive used to give up to three kilos of honey, and now gives one or two. With flowers blooming at different times, the honey has also turned bitter.
The report also notes that in many areas women who are menstruating are forbidden from going near the hives. So the women whose labour keeps the hive going often have no right to take its honey.
nazar: This story is the other face of migration from the hills. When villages empty out, the burden of farming, cattle, forest fires and now even pollination falls on women, with no recognition or help. Without the native bee, farming in the hills will grow weaker too.

If government housing and beekeeping schemes made room for local knowledge, wall hives could be built in new houses as well. For that, we first have to ask the women who have done this work for generations.
sawal: Why is there no room for bees in the wall of a concrete house?
ref: Apis cerana indica
Asia's native honeybee, which can bear the mountain cold. It gives less honey than the European bee but matters greatly for pollinating local crops and forests.
Phag
Traditional songs of Kumaon, sung at weddings and festivals. According to the report, some phag songs are about bees.

h: Navi Pillay: from granddaughter of indentured labourers to a Nobel, a fight for justice
dek: 2026 Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay talks to Democracy Now about US sanctions on the International Criminal Court, Gaza, and the fight to make rape in war a crime.
body: Navi Pillay, the South African lawyer and international judge, has won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. In this conversation of about half an hour, she speaks from The Hague with Democracy Now's Amy Goodman and Juan González. The interview took place on the same day the United States announced new sanctions on the International Criminal Court.

Pillay says she heard about the prize in Nuremberg, during a conference in the same Courtroom 600 where Nazi leaders were tried after the Second World War. She also points out that very few women have won this prize so far.

She flatly rejects the US sanctions. She says the work of an international court should not be stopped at the will of a powerful country. The UN commission of inquiry on Gaza that she led concluded that Israel had committed genocide. Pillay says that report was made on a UN mandate, written after examining the facts, and names the leaders who should be put on trial.

An important part of the conversation is about Rwanda. As a judge at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, Pillay was part of the Akayesu case, which for the first time set a broad definition of rape and sexual violence and held that such violence can be part of the intent to commit genocide. She explains why that ruling became a milestone.

She also talks about her roots. Her grandparents were girmitiya (indentured) labourers on sugarcane plantations. Facing discrimination in apartheid South Africa, she finished her studies with help from her community. She also says the United States opposed her appointment as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights in 2008, which she believes was because of her stand on women's reproductive rights.

At the end she tells the story of Robben Island, where through a court case she won legal rights for political prisoners. Later Nelson Mandela made her the first Black woman judge of South Africa's High Court.
nazar: Navi Pillay's life carries the memory of indentured labourers taken from India to the sugarcane fields, the fight against apartheid, and a stubborn insistence on holding international law up against powerful countries. At a time when international courts are being sanctioned, her Nobel is a reminder that the measure of justice must be the same for everyone.

There is a lesson in it for India too. The understanding built by the Rwanda tribunal, that sexual violence is a weapon of power and hate, is vital for justice for Dalit, Adivasi and minority women in every case, from Manipur to the riots.
sawal: If the court is sanctioned, who will hold genocide to account?
ref: Akayesu case
A 1998 ruling of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. For the first time, rape was recognised as a means of committing genocide.
Girmitiya
Labourers taken from India in the nineteenth century, on an agreement (the 'girmit'), to work on plantations in colonies such as Mauritius, Fiji and South Africa.

h: Firaq's poetry and the darkness in his home
dek: On Samalochan, Amita Sheereen reads Alka Sahai Pathak's biography of Firaq Gorakhpuri and asks how to make sense of a great poet's treatment of his wife and children.
body: Raghupati Sahai 'Firaq' Gorakhpuri is counted among the very greatest Urdu poets. Alka Sahai Pathak, from his family, has written his biography in English, published by Om Books International. On Samalochan, Amita Sheereen uses this book to step into the part of the poet's life about which literary gatherings usually stay silent.

The story begins with his marriage in 1914. Firaq, then eighteen, had insisted that the bride be beautiful and educated, and his father, the lawyer-poet Ibrat Gorakhpuri, had agreed. On the wedding day Firaq was disappointed when he saw Kishori Devi, and according to the author this resentment lasted all his life. His wife was sent back to her parents' home and called, twenty years later, to the house on Bank Road in Allahabad, where every night brought drink and abuse.

He was just as cold to his children. When his daughter Prabha went through typhoid he showed no grief, and even after his nineteen-year-old son Govind died in 1937, the mother was not allowed to put up his photograph. After his father's death he took charge of the Lakshmi Niwas mansion; his mother, brothers and sisters had to live in the cowshed, and the mansion was sold cheaply. After his younger daughter Pushpa married in 1954, he separated from his wife.

But the picture is not one-sided. He was very gentle with other people's children. He spent a year in jail during the Non-Cooperation Movement, was joint secretary of the Congress from 1922 to 1927, and died in Delhi in 1982.

Amita Sheereen looks separately at a contradictory personality, a broken mind and mental illness. In her view, Firaq's behaviour can only be understood within the frame of feudal arranged marriage and patriarchy, in which an ego that thought itself very great may have reached the point of illness. She also questions the progressive circles that kept singing the poet's praises and forgot Kishori Devi. Her conclusion: Firaq was a wonderful poet and also a social tragedy.
nazar: The debate about separating art from the artist is not new, but in the Hindi-Urdu world it often becomes an excuse to protect a big name. The strength of this essay is that, without making Firaq's poetry any smaller, it brings to the centre the woman whose life became the price of that poetry. How many Kishori Devis were never recorded in our literary history at all? Every biography should be asked that question.
sawal: In which of Firaq's verses is Kishori Devi's story recorded?
ref: Firaq Gorakhpuri
Raghupati Sahai (1896-1982), Urdu poet and teacher of English at Allahabad University. The first Urdu writer to win the Jnanpith, for 'Gul-e-Naghma' (Flower of Song).
Narcissism
A tendency to think oneself extremely important and to be indifferent to others' pain. When severe, psychology treats it as a personality disorder.

h: Farewell to Ved Rahi: an old woman's voice in an empty village
dek: On Sammukh, Yogita Yadav remembers the great Dogri storyteller Ved Rahi through a Hindi translation of his story 'Aawazein' (Voices), about a village emptied by shelling across the border.
body: According to Sammukh, the Jammu writer and filmmaker Ved Rahi died on 1 November. Born in 1933, Rahi was the son of Lala Mulkhraj Saraf, one of the early figures of journalism in Jammu and Kashmir, who brought out the newspaper 'Ranbir'. Rahi began writing in Urdu, then went on to write in Hindi and Dogri.

His story collection 'Aale' won the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1983. His novel 'Lal Ded' is about the fourteenth-century saint-poet of Kashmir and has been translated into many languages. In films he worked a great deal with Ramanand Sagar, wrote the story, screenplay or dialogue for about twenty-five films, directed a few, and made the Doordarshan serial 'Gul Gulshan Gulfam'.

As a tribute, the writer Yogita Yadav has brought one of his stories into Hindi. It is night, the village is silent, the houses are dark. An old woman, leaning on a stick, goes from door to door calling her neighbours by name, scolding one, lost in memories of another.

Slowly we learn that after shelling from across the border the whole village has fled, and she alone is left. Her daughter Lajo is gone too. Her anger turns to fear; she goes back home, hurts herself, and is left asking when the people will come back. Nothing big happens in the story, there are only voices that get no answer.
Yogita Yadav recently also brought a work by Padma Sachdev into Hindi on Sammukh. This effort to take Dogri literature to Hindi readers gives Rahi's memory its proper shape.
nazar: People of border areas like Poonch, Rajouri or RS Pura appear in national debates only as numbers: how many shells fell, how many homes emptied. Rahi's story shows that the real price of war is paid by the old and the women who cannot run. Little literature from languages like Dogri reaches Hindi, and translations like this take us to voices that the war-talk of TV drowns out.
sawal: After the shelling, who is it that stays behind in the village?
ref: Dogri
The language of the Jammu region, added to the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution in 2003.
Lal Ded
Lalleshwari, the fourteenth-century Kashmiri saint-poet, whose 'vakhs' (verses) are seen as the foundation of Kashmiri literature.

h: The diary said 'writer'; the family read 'fahisha'
dek: On Sammukh, the new instalment of poet Neha Naruka's prose series 'Mritatmaon ka Desh' tells of a girl's body seen in childhood and of the label stuck on women who speak up.
body: Neha Naruka is a Hindi poet; 'Phati Hatheliyan' (Cracked Palms) is her poetry collection, and she received the Vagishwari Samman in 2024. On Sammukh she is writing a prose series called 'Mritatmaon ka Desh' (Land of the Dead), in which each instalment grows out of the memory of someone who has died. This instalment is the 'death-story' of a girl named Fahisha, and it stands somewhere between memoir and fiction.

It begins with a strange game: the narrator keeps the dead preserved in her mind like mummies. Then comes a hospital scene, where a sister-in-law who has been burnt is dying and relatives are loudly putting on a show of sympathy. Some time after she is gone, a new sister-in-law arrives in the house.

The real story lies in summer holidays at her mother's parents' village. The girls play games with dolls: weddings, pregnancy and funerals. One evening the whole village runs towards the fields, where Fahisha's body lies, and it seems she has been murdered. The child sees it all in pieces: clothes, jewellery, nail polish, dried blood. The whispers that follow haunt her for years.

As she grows up, Fahisha keeps returning in her poems, which makes readers and colleagues uneasy. Then society starts calling her a fahisha too, because she speaks out and lives as she chooses. The goal she wrote in her diary, to become a writer, her family reads as that very label.

The piece shows how the village and the family police a woman's tongue, her clothes and her 'honour', and how a neighbour's remark can make violence against a daughter seem almost justified. In the end the rain washes the word off the walls, but the memory does not fade. For the writer, to keep telling the stories of the dead is the way to stay alive.
nazar: The death of a girl killed in a village stays a whisper, and her name becomes an insult: this is the whole machinery of violence in the name of 'honour'. Neha Naruka's prose shows that a woman who writes and speaks is frightened with that very label. As long as women's voices are taken for loose character, such bodies will keep turning up in fields and their stories will survive only in poems.
sawal: If the rain washes the word from the wall, does the label wash away too?
ref: Fahisha
A word of Arabic-Urdu origin, used as an insult for a woman seen as immoral.
Mritatmaon ka Desh
Neha Naruka's prose series on Sammukh; each instalment grows out of the memory of a character who has died.

h: The beatings behind the closed walls of rich homes
dek: Shivani Sibal's novel 'Moms' shows that money and status do not stop domestic violence.
body: Set in Delhi's well-off homes, Shivani Sibal's new novel 'Moms' is split into two parts, before Radhika is gone and after. We learn at the very start that Radhika took her own life, so the shadow of that emptiness falls over the whole story.

Radhika is a full-time wife and mother. Her husband Manik is a lawyer whose world is limited to his work and his earnings. Their daughter Samara wants her mother not to turn up everywhere at school, and to find a life of her own, a job. Radhika gets a little authority on the school's parent committee, where she sits down to teach other parents origami she learnt from the internet, and a working mother, Ipsita, mocks her strictness.

As confident as she is outside, she is just as helpless at home. If Manik does not like her hair, he cuts it; he locks her in a dark room as punishment and makes her take pills to lose weight. At a party, in front of friends, he punches her. A childhood memory also surfaces, of her mother punishing her, as if she had been taught long ago to bear cruelty.

The reviewer finds some characters incomplete. Even after Radhika's death, Manik does not change at all. The 1984 anti-Sikh riots appear in the background of Tara, the yoga teacher, but do not connect with her life today, and her disabled husband never gets a voice. Modi compares Manik with Aahan from Sibal's first novel 'Equations': both use their anger as an excuse for violence against women.

Still, the novel is funny even while it is heavy, as when Radhika's mother gets her hair set before the condolence meeting. According to the reviewer, the book is a mirror for rich readers, and for everyone else a glimpse of the loneliness that grows inside wealth.
nazar: In India domestic violence is often taken to be a story of poverty, drink and 'uneducated' men. This novel breaks that comfortable illusion. In big houses the marks of beating hide under expensive clothes and status, and a woman's financial dependence makes her even more alone.

A woman who gives up her own income to run the house is left with no way out either. Talk of the domestic violence law and counselling will work only when we accept that this is a sickness of every class.
sawal: Manik cuts Radhika's hair; why does no neighbour ask?
ref: Domestic Violence Act 2005

A law that protects women from physical, mental and economic violence inside the home.
It includes protection orders and the right to live in the shared household.
1984 anti-Sikh riots

The mass killing of Sikhs in Delhi and several other cities after Indira Gandhi's assassination.
Thousands were killed, and justice remains incomplete to this day.
photo_note: Shakuntala lost in thought, Ravi Varma

h: Begum Hazrat Mahal, on the margins of her own story
dek: Rosie Llewellyn-Jones's new biography brings Awadh's rebel Begum into view, but through men's eyes.
body: Historian Rosie Llewellyn-Jones has a new book on Begum Hazrat Mahal, who took command of Awadh in the 1857 revolt. Pragya Mittal considers it important, but complains that the Begum arrives late in the book. First come Wajid Ali Shah, the court and her son Birjis Qadr, and only then, somewhere, the woman whose name the book bears.

The reviewer reminds us that even her real name has been lost. 'Mahal' was a title Wajid Ali Shah gave to women he favoured, and 'Hazrat' an honorific. Her mother is said to have been a slave, and an African origin is also guessed at, but nothing is certain. Dancer, muta wife, Birjis's mother: many such identities turn up, but little of the person.

Still, the picture of the days of the revolt is powerful. Her son was king in name; real rule was the Begum's. She held court, raised money, and kept together soldiers, landlords and religious leaders who distrusted one another. Even after Lucknow fell in March 1858, the fighting went on in the countryside, and she openly answered Queen Victoria's proclamation, saying do not trust the British.

She turned down a British pension, went to Nepal and never returned to Awadh. She died of fever in Kathmandu. When the Sunni graveyard there would not take the Shia Begum, the prime minister of Nepal gave separate land.

According to Mittal, the most stinging thing is a note by a British officer who, on hearing of her death, asks whether this was the same Begum who had taken a leading part in the revolt. The book begins with men and ends with men, and the Begum is still waiting for a history with herself at its centre.
nazar: In our history of the freedom struggle, Rani Lakshmibai found a place, but a Shia Begum, the daughter of a mother who was probably a slave, and called a dancer, has not received the same respect. The triple blow of caste, religion and being a woman shows up among the writers of history too.
Today, when there are attempts to turn Awadh and the Mughal era into villains, Hazrat Mahal's story reminds us that Muslim women were among those who fought the longest battle against the British.
sawal: Who gave land in Kathmandu for the Begum's grave?
ref: Birjis Qadr

The son of Wajid Ali Shah and Hazrat Mahal, whom the rebels made king of Awadh in 1857.
He later went to Nepal with his mother.
Muta nikah

A fixed-term marriage in the Shia tradition.
In the age of the Nawabs, there were many such wives at court.
photo_note: A nineteenth-century begum, a Kalighat painting

h: Pakistan's 'deep state': the army is not the only one to blame
dek: Ahmad Faruqui's review of Moonis Ahmar's new book asks how a structure that has not changed in 79 years will change in 21.
body: Pakistan was created as a home for the Muslims of British India, with the dream of a secular and democratic country. But within twenty-five years it broke apart and moved far from what its founders had in mind. Moonis Ahmar's new book examines this journey: how Pakistan became a 'deep state'. In Dawn, the economist Ahmad Faruqui has reviewed it.

According to Ahmar, the army has seized power four times since 1958 and ruled directly for a total of 33 years. Ayub Khan had said as early as 1954 that politicians were not fit to run the country, and four years later he overthrew the government. After 2008 the army kept running things from behind the curtain, with the bureaucracy and the political elite on its side. It also built business organisations run by serving or retired officers.

The most interesting thing about the book is that Ahmar does not put all the blame on the army. Clerics, tribal chiefs, landlords, industrialists and the bureaucracy were all part of this alliance, which put military security above the safety of ordinary people. Governments fell again and again in the first eleven years, so people welcomed Ayub's coup, and the army kept its image as 'the country's guardian'.

Ahmar explains the idea of the 'deep state' with examples from Egypt, Russia, Turkey and the United States, and suggests paths up to 2047: roll back the constitutional amendments that cemented the army's role, free the courts, allow free speech, and spend on society before the defence budget.

Faruqui sees this as a very big ask. His question is why a strategic mindset that has not changed in 79 years would change in 21, especially when earlier popular uprisings failed. He complains that the definition of 'deep state' comes too late and that examples are repeated, but he still finds the book thought-provoking.
nazar: This book is not only about the state of a neighbour. When a country places 'national security' above every question, the first to pay the price are the poor, workers, minorities and people from the margins. In India too, budgets, laws and the room for debate are shrinking in the name of security.

Ahmar's most useful point is that such a structure is not built by the uniform alone; it needs the support of religion, capital, landlordism and the bureaucracy. Recognising this alliance is the first condition for saving democracy.
sawal: Why did clerics, landlords and businessmen stand with the army?
ref: Deep state
A network of the army, intelligence agencies and bureaucracy behind the elected government that makes the real decisions and does not answer to the people.
Basic Democracies
Ayub Khan's 1959 system, in which people elected the president not directly but through elected local representatives.

h: On rally day, the BJP hits back: 'orders came from abroad', and the question of the 1984 riots anniversary
dek: While the opposition rallied on vote theft, the BJP took out a Save Democracy march in Delhi and alleged the rally was deliberately held on the anniversary of the 1984 anti-Sikh riots.
pub: From a report in The Wire
body: Two kinds of politics ran side by side in Delhi on 1 November. As the opposition gathered at Ramlila Maidan over vote theft and its demand for the election commissioner's resignation, the BJP took out a 'Save Democracy, Remove Anarchy' march the same day. Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta led it.

The BJP's main attack was on the date of the rally. The party said 1, 2 and 3 November are the days when the anti-Sikh riots took place in 1984, and holding a rally on such a day was like rubbing salt into the wounds of riot victims. Union Home Minister Amit Shah said in Chandigarh that the BJP had earlier asked the opposition to change the date, but it had refused.

Shah also said instructions for the rally had come from abroad. His remark was among the sharpest political comments of the day, because it accused the opposition not just of political opposition but of acting on an outside signal. BJP president J. P. Nadda too alleged that Rahul Gandhi had forgotten the martyrs for his own politics.

The opposition rejected these charges. It said the date had been fixed in advance and that giving the rally a communal colour was the BJP's strategy. The opposition also said the BJP was raising other issues to distract from the questions over the Election Commission.

Another side of the day was the BJP's claim that chairs in front of the stage were empty during Rahul Gandhi's speech, while organisers and reports described a large crowd. Along with the rally's news, then, there was politics over its image too, which is the mark of today's media age: the frame is set before the truth.
nazar: The BJP's counter was sharp, but its focus was the rally's date and a count of chairs, not the questions over the Election Commission. That is a sign of its strategy: when the other side has a paper trail, question its morality and its crowd.
The lesson for the opposition is that sensitive anniversaries have to be kept in mind when choosing a rally date. Otherwise, however strong the issue, the opponent can bring it down to a single date.
sawal: Does questioning the rally's date weaken the Election Commission issue, or is it only political noise?
ref: The 1984 riots

After Indira Gandhi's assassination on 31 October 1984, anti-Sikh riots broke out in Delhi and some other cities, in which thousands were killed. Events of mourning and remembrance are held every year from 1 to 3 November.
ank: day, two different kinds of politics

h: M. A. Baby: this is a second freedom struggle, and it belongs to no single party
dek: The CPI(M) general secretary called the rally a second struggle for independence. He recalled the history of Ramlila Maidan and said the crowd was saying one thing: their fascist ways will not work here.
body: At the rally, CPI(M) general secretary M. A. Baby made the broadest political claim on behalf of the Left parties. He said the sea of people gathered at Ramlila Maidan were all saying one thing to Modi, Amit Shah and Gyanesh Kumar: your fascist ways will not work in India.

Baby recalled the historic legacy of the ground. He said leaders like Mahatma Gandhi, B. R. Ambedkar, Jawaharlal Nehru and Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel had spoken here. Gathering here today, then, is not a new political event but a continuation of that tradition.
He said this is a second struggle for independence, fought to save the country from the fascist hands of the RSS. He repeated the demand for Gyanesh Kumar's resignation and for a case against him.

Baby said Gandhi had chosen the path of satyagraha, while Modi is choosing the path of lies. He recalled the promise to farmers that their incomes would double, and said incomes did not double but farmer suicides rose.
His speech was different in that he did not keep the fight limited to the Election Commission but placed it within the larger frame of the Constitution, secularism and civil rights.
nazar: Calling it a 'second freedom struggle' is an emotionally enormous claim. It fills workers with energy, but in comparing with history one must also remember that the freedom struggle risked lives, while this is a fight for the right to vote.
The most useful part of Baby's speech was his insistence that this is everyone's movement. For the Left that is also necessary, because its street politics alone no longer carries mass weight.
sawal: Does calling it a 'second freedom struggle' give the movement moral strength, or does the comparison with history weaken it?
ref: Ramlila Maidan

h: Farooq Abdullah: Muslims have shed blood for this country, stop calling them 'Pakistanis'
dek: The National Conference president objected to questions about Muslims' patriotism. He asked: if Hindus' names have been struck off the voter roll, would they be called Pakistanis too?
body: At the rally, National Conference president Farooq Abdullah raised the question of Muslim identity and citizenship. He said Muslims have shed blood for the country and will keep doing so, and yet they are repeatedly humiliated by being called Pakistanis.

He accused the BJP of targeting Muslims again and again. His question was: if Hindus' names have been removed from the voter roll, would they be called Pakistanis too? He asked it not only for the sake of argument but to show who the 'infiltrator' label is meant for.

He said India's Constitution gives all citizens equal rights, and that people need to struggle, not live in fear. He also said those sitting silent today must understand that silence only encourages others.
Abdullah said at the rally that the condition of democracy in Jammu and Kashmir, and in the rest of the country, is a warning for everyone. He appealed to the opposition to stay united.
His speech mattered because he tied the voter-roll issue to minority citizenship. That link turns the movement from an electoral fight into a fight for civil rights.
nazar: Abdullah's was the sharpest political question of the day, because it cornered the government's 'infiltrator' language on its own ground. For the community that is doubted in every election, that question is both relief and courage.

But it is also true that the question of why minorities should have to prove their patriotism at all should have been raised. Until it is, the terms of the debate will remain the ones the government has set.
